extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of literature, social criticism, and cultural history
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from a 19th/early-20th century literary-history/social-criticism essay combining short fictional vignettes, a club-scene narrative, reflections on ethics and religion, a short book review, and a reader-advice column. The passage advances arguments about domestic organization, gendered ethics, religion, and standards for public speech and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern domestic economy / centralized household services
rubrics_metrics.description: Every family is a distinct unit ... the separate home may be served by a common water company, by a common milkman, by a common baker, by a common cooking and a common cleaning establishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that individual household inefficiencies and waste (individual purchasing, duplicate kitchen furnishings, servant problems) can be greatly reduced by outsourcing or centralizing services: kitchenless houses served by skilled hourly labor, ordering food cooked instead of raw, common carriers and competent wholesale purchasing; this will save about two-thirds of living expenses, elevate domestic service into a respected profession with well-paid employees, and solve the 'servant question.' Anti-pattern: small groups combining households ('co-operative housekeeping') driven together because none can manage alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-operative housekeeping is not a panacea
rubrics_metrics.description: The inefficiency of a dozen tottering households is not removed by combining them. Why should we expect a group of families to 'keep house' expertly and economically together, when they are driven into companionship by the fact that none of them can do it alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining inefficient households without providing competent centralized management does not solve inefficiency; solutions should rely on professional organization and specialization rather than mere aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of club/meeting decorum and parliamentary procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Order! You will please keep order. ... I move you, Madam President, that a resolution of condemnation be passed at once; and the meeting then dismissed!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage shows expected procedures for an organized club meeting: maintenance of order, recognition of speakers, formal motions and seconds, use of the gavel, votes, and respectful treatment of invited speakers (a vote of thanks). Anti-patterns and penalties: gross discourtesy to a guest, disorderly hissing, frenzied motions to adjourn, expulsions or resignations resulting from breach of decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for effective public speaking and persuasive presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Both employer and employed!--and gentlemen--whom I am delighted to see here to-day! I am grateful for the opportunity ... of listening to the most rational, practical, wise and hopeful words I have ever heard on this subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective speeches are praised for being rational, practical, wise, hopeful, scholarly and clearly presented by someone 'who knows.' Such qualities win approval, applause, and can persuade a divided audience. Speakers who are plain, practical, and authoritative gain credibility; anti-patterns include frivolous, dangerous, or ill-informed presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics as a science of social relations (evaluate by effects on human welfare)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethics is the science of social relation, how persons and social forces work with and on one another. Ethics and religion are distinctly human concerns; they belong to us as social factors, not as physical ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author advocates treating ethics analytically—like physics for the material world—by observing effects of conduct and deriving principles that promote human welfare. Ethical laws should be judged by their contribution to human well-being and social flourishing rather than by mere tradition or taboo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive/taboo-based ethics versus cultivated positive ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Primitive ethics consists mostly of Tabus—the things that are forbidden; and all our dim notions of ethics to this day, as well as most of our religions, deal mainly with forbidding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the historical predominance of prohibitions in early ethics and the need to develop positive, cultivated virtues and habits. Move from a dominance of 'Thou shalt not' to an ethical system that prescribes constructive actions for human betterment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge moral rules by their human utility, not by sexed enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Chastity is a virtue because it promotes human welfare--not because men happen to prize it in women. The underlying reason for the whole thing is the benefit of the child; and to that end a pure and noble fatherhood is requisite, as well as such a motherhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral rules should be evaluated on whether they promote human welfare (e.g., the welfare of children), and enforced consistently across sexes. The text condemns double standards (punishing women but excusing men) and argues for impartial application of ethical norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique androcentric bias in ethics, law, and religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Man, as a sex, has quite naturally deified his own qualities rather than those of his opposite. In his codes of manners, of morals, of laws ... we see masculinity written large on every side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cultural, legal, and religious systems for male-centered assumptions and biases. Favor human-centered standards that leave 'sex characteristics where they belong' and judge ethical/religious systems by their universality and fairness rather than masculine instinct or tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use status and freedom of women as a measure of religious and social progressiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The wider and deeper the religion, the more it calls for practical applications ... the more it appeals to women. Further ... progressiveness is to be measured, not by the numbers of its women adherents, but by their relative freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a religion or social system's progressiveness, consider the degree of practical application of its teachings and the relative freedom and status it affords to women; anti-patterns include religions or systems that preserve servile womanhood and resist adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'combat' metaphor in moral growth; prefer growth and cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: This combat theory ... made moral growth an everlasting battle. This is a masculine error; growth is the major process, combat only a subsidiary one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reframe moral education and social development in terms of growth and habit-formation rather than perpetual struggle. Beware of over-emphasizing conflict as the organizing metaphor for ethics, law, or education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for strong nonfiction/social-critique writing (from book review)
rubrics_metrics.description: He has clear eyes and a silver tongue. His perceptions are important and his expressions convincing. He speaks plainly also ... Plenty of epigrams in the book, plenty of imagination, plenty of hard sense; and some mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A persuasive nonfiction work should show perceptiveness (clear eyes), eloquence (a 'silver tongue'), convincing expression, plain and direct speech, a balance of imagination and practical sense, memorable epigrams, and honesty about limitations or mistakes. Reviewers should notice both strengths and errors; effective use of examples and forceful phrasing enhances impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice on handling socially burdensome guests (boundary-setting as a social skill)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only real cure is courage on the part of the victim. If the suffering host or hostess frankly said, 'My dear Sir--or Madam--you are making me very tired. I wish you would go away,' the result would leave nothing to be desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When social interactions harm one's well-being, direct, candid boundary-setting is recommended. The trade-off is reputational or relational risk—decide whether you prefer to keep the person visiting or to assert the boundary and risk their not returning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose unfair gendered expectations in filial duty
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are a man, your duty is to provide a home for the patient, a servant, a nurse, a physician, food, medicine, and two short calls a day. ... If you are a woman, you need provide none of these things; but must wait upon the patient with your own hands as nurse and servant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage highlights and critiques normative expectations that assign material provision to men and personal caregiving to women; an evaluative standard here is fairness in assigning duties regardless of sex and recognition of individual capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic suffrage criterion: intelligent participation of all people
rubrics_metrics.description: A true democracy requires the intelligent participation of all the people, and that women are people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support for full suffrage is grounded in the view that democracy only functions well when all adult members—women included—participate intelligently in government; the standard for enfranchisement is citizenship plus capacity for informed participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of fashion/market-driven discomfort (form over function)
rubrics_metrics.description: The desire for novelty; the lack of a real feeling for beauty; a savage indifference to physical comfort ... all these combine to make our feet ugly and painful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate fashions and market-driven design by their impact on human comfort and beauty; criticize practices that prioritize novelty and sales over ergonomics and well-being.
